rows.description: I am furious at being dropped and rehearse cutting replies. Wise: let the anger cool, decide whether the friendship is worth one calm message, and keep my dignity.

A close friend stopped replying with no reason and I replay everything I said. Wise: send one honest message, then accept the silence and stop chasing. Harmful: blaming myself or messaging fifty times.
They reply only when it suits them and I keep waiting. Wise: say what I need; if it does not change, step back. Harmful: lowering my standards and calling it patience.
My friend moved on to new people and treats me as background. I am hurt but see that friendships shift with time. Wise: name it once, then invest in new and reciprocal bonds.

A colleague and I compete for the same promotion and I feel tense and calculating. I focus on my work and visible results, stay honest, and do not sabotage; rivalry can sharpen me if it does not poison my character.

A colleague covered for me during a family emergency and I feel indebted. I thank them sincerely and return the favour at the right time; a workplace of mutual help is worth more than any single task.

I look down on a slower colleague and roll my eyes in meetings. I see that contempt says more about my stress and pride than their worth, and I choose to help or set clear expectations instead of mocking.
You worry and want to know everything about your child. Wise: trust builds by letting them make small mistakes. Harmful: surveillance or shaming.

rows.subtype: Parents × Divorce or conflict at home [Receiver]
rows.description: Their fights or separation land on you. Wise: it is not your job to fix them, and you can love both while keeping healthy distance. Harmful: taking a side in the war.
They track your spending or use funds as leverage. Wise: negotiate a clear budget, share information, and build your own income. Harmful: lying or manipulating them for money.

You rely on them for fees and rent and feel you cannot speak freely. Wise: work toward some earning, use money wisely, and do not confuse support with control. Immature: spending carelessly and resenting them.
A toddler stares at the phone, goes still and screams when it is taken. The fast lights hijack attention. Limit and share it with a caregiver, and offer play, hands-on activity and outdoor time.
When the screen is turned off the child throws herself on the floor. It is sadness and frustration, not manners. Stay calm, hold the limit, offer a hug and a new activity.
When the parent hands over the phone to keep the child quiet, the child gets stimulation but not a person. Caregivers should treat it as a tool, not a babysitter, and talk and play daily.
Rules feel unfair and complex, and you resent paying. It is fine to dislike a system while complying with it and voting or advocating for change. Evasion turns a grievance into a legal risk.

Someone offers to make the problem vanish for a fee and shortcuts. Recognise a common exploit: bribery is illegal and leaves you exposed and owned. Use certified professionals and official portals, and ask for receipts.

A notice from the tax office makes your heart race and imagination run wild. Read it carefully, note deadlines, gather documents, and consult a qualified professional. Panic-paying agents or ignoring it worsens things.
Treat the process as a system with rules, not a personal attack. Respond on time, be accurate, and be polite in writing. Dealing honestly with authority usually costs less than hiding.
People praise you suddenly and ask for favours. Notice the pattern, thank them, and check whether they were around before. Keep truthful friends who can tell you when you are wrong.

A friend congratulates you but seems sour, or teases you about your new status. Stay humble, avoid showing off, and keep the friendship anchored in shared history. Give them space, and share their wins too.

Success brings impostor feelings and fear of being found out. Recognise that many capable people feel it. Keep a record of achievements, ask for feedback, and continue learning without pretending to know everything.
The success was built by others, too. Thank them by name, share credit and rewards, and mention their contributions to senior leaders. A leader who takes all the credit slowly loses trusted people.
